articles.title: She voted for Trump every time. Then came cancer and the bills
articles.summary: McALLEN, Texas (AP) — The Ford Expedition rumbled to a stop and Cindy Banda’s bedazzled flip-flops landed on the asphalt of the Houston cancer center’s vast...
articles.body:
Election 2026 Cancer Patient Photo Essay

McALLEN, Texas (AP) — The Ford Expedition rumbled to a stop and Cindy Banda's bedazzled flip-flops landed on the asphalt of the Houston cancer center's vast parking lot. She threaded through the rows of cars, a tally of patients who gather here to sit with chemotherapy needles or lie on radiation machines.

The elevator dinged open. A year ago in this building, surgeons removed Banda's right breast, and she still didn't know whether treatment had expunged the cancer from her body. Doctors had told her it would be tough to beat.

"I'm more of a positive person myself," Banda said, now sitting with a white wristband in a dim waiting room. But the bills are harder to dismiss, and the single mother with six children in her care repeated something like a mantra. "Keep the house. Keep the cars. And just keep the kids stable."

That's true for many Americans, as rising healthcare costs leave more families with a sinking feeling after seeing the bill for surgery or medication. Heading into the Nov. 3 midterm elections, about half of registered voters said healthcare costs are a major problem for them and their families, up from a little more than one-third four years ago, according to a Fox News poll from September.

With party control of Congress at stake, registered voters are nearly twice as likely to say they trust Democrats over Republicans to handle healthcare , according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll from the same month. Those frustrations, combined with broader concerns over rising prices, have sapped support for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

Banda knows how that feels. She backed Trump in each of his three campaigns, motivated by her opposition to abortion . But when cancer came, the ensuing scramble to make ends meet was painful enough to rearrange her priorities, and she started to think about voting Democratic for the first time.

The 46-year-old was ushered into a sterile room for her appointment, her phone lit up with a text. "Please contact TD Auto Finance."

"This one's $1,300," she said of the car payment bill. "I have to go back to work."

She had been on sick leave from her job selling internet service for one year, and she needed the income to support her three kids and three more she had taken in after her sister's death.

The doctor said her reconstruction surgery could be scheduled early next year. "I was hoping for maybe December," Banda said, "only because I've met my deductibles." Come January, she would have to pay down the $7,500 again. Earlier may be possible, the doctor replied, if the skin around her surgical scar loosens.

The evening had cooled slightly by the time she walked back through the rows of parked cars, their ebb and flow marking the tide of sickness, survival and death in a small corner of a colossal healthcare industry that saves lives while taking in over $5 trillion every year.

Confronting death and debt in America before a midterm election

Two weeks later, Banda was back at work, making door-to-door rounds to sell Spectrum's Wi-Fi in McAllen, her city along the U.S.-Mexico border in the Rio Grande Valley. Banda, holding blue flyers, walked along a row of storefronts, some that shuttered since she last was in the area.

She hadn't had a sale and commission since October of last year, after the biopsy and diagnosis.

The doctor who gave her the news had hugged Banda, and she sobbed even though she never really sobs in front of other people. During chemo, her children took turns buzzing off her wispy hair. When her 9-year-old daughter's hand quivered, a teenage cousin helped guide the clipper over her mother's scalp.

Banda's first impulse was to maintain normalcy, stability, for the children.

But that requires roughly $7,000 a month for utilities, mortgage, car payments and groceries, along with the two water leaks. Then, even with insurance through her job, the surgeries, chemo and radiation added up to over $25,000 that she's been paying off, making Banda one of tens of millions of other people in the United States in medical debt.

Banda tries not to dwell on death and debt.

"It'll consume you," she says. She smothers those thoughts beneath her bubbly demeanor and avoids being alone. But that truce, between her insistence on positivity and the fears that it covers, is brittle.

Certain thoughts still arrive uninvited. Banda's late sister, Melissa, didn't have life insurance. Banda makes sure it's a payment she never misses.

"Sometimes I think, and I shouldn't think like this, but I'm worth more gone than here," she said one day. "Obviously, the goal is not that, the goal is to beat it," she continued, "to keep the house and keep the cars."

So far she has, with the help of others.

On top of child support, the father of Banda's 9-year-old often pays $400 a week for a nanny to help with the kids. Banda's own father sent her $700 before for her recent Houston appointment, one of his many cash infusions. Her high school classmates, who she hadn't been in close touch with in decades, fundraised by selling grilled chicken, rice and beans from a roadside tent. Two GoFundMe fundraisers raised nearly $30,000 and Banda rented her late sister's house while putting her own in forbearance.

But months of insecurity takes its own, sleepless toll. She needed to sell some internet services to catch up.

After sticking the Spectrum Wi-Fi flyers onto empty storefronts, she drove to pick up her kids from school. The following day she had a morning meeting at a barbershop for what would be her first sale back at work.

Turning on Trump and voting Democratic for the first time

A lifelong Christian, Banda had voted her anti-abortion stance in past elections. When her sister was kidnapped and murdered by her ex-husband in 2020, Banda retreated from religion. The cancer brought her back to church with an apology to God, but it also made her rethink her politics.

She voted for Trump in 2016, and his first four years seemed steady, so she voted for him again in 2020. Democratic President Joe Biden's tenure, including the tail end of a global pandemic and rising inflation, felt like bedlam, so she voted for Trump to return to the White House in 2024.

But two years later and fighting an expensive disease, she had found no respite from high prices.

So when James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminary student running for U.S. Senate as a Democrat, visited one of Banda's fundraisers — speaking about his diabetes and his work in the Texas Statehouse to lower the price of insulin — it moved her. "Imagine if he can do that for the cancer," she said.

Talarico and his Republican opponent, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, have different approaches to healthcare. Talarico wants all Americans to be able to join Medicare; Paxton proposed a $25,000 tax deduction for out-of-pocket medical expenses.

Talarico also supports a law guaranteeing abortion access nationwide, which Banda has voted against for years. But after she slid into debt to stay alive, after her grocery bills mounted and the high school had to comp the kids' soccer gear she couldn't afford, Banda's anti-abortion concerns have been superseded by costs.

"Because it's what I'm living," she said. "I'm living it."

Banda cast an early ballot for Talarico. "Never voted Democrat before today!!" she wrote in a text with blue heart emoji.

Her news will come on Election Day, in a doctor's office

Banda had just started a new cancer-targeting medication that cost $16,000 a month, reduced to $500 by insurance. By the afternoon, she was nauseous and fatigued, unable to eat. The malaise would keep her home the next day. She would miss the meeting with the barbershop to close her first deal since getting sick, though she felt confident it was in the bag.

But Banda pushed through the discomfort one evening to join her family as they replaced the flowers at her sister's tomb.

She drove past the headstones and oak trees in the evening's slanting light, and the family gathered around Melissa Banda's tomb in an open-air mausoleum. There was no speech. Their eulogy was her father, Fidel Banda, methodically clipping and arranging the flowers for his daughter.

Banda walked along the wall of tombs. She will find out on Election Day whether the cancer is in remission or whether it's spread to her organs.

"This one's for me," she said, pointing to a blank tomb next to her sister's.

"Mom!" said her daughter with the huffiness of a 9-year-old. "Why would you say that?"

Banda smiled and added, "in a hundred years."

articles.title: UK PM Burnham says he wants to discuss a return to EU freedom of movement
articles.summary: Burnham says Britain should have an ‘honest discussion’ about how immigration to the UK has changed since Brexit.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he wants to discuss Britain returning to the European Union’s freedom of movement rules for workers, a key issue in the 2016 Brexit referendum which led to the United Kingdom leaving the bloc.

Addressing the need to rethink ties with Brussels, ⁠Burnham told The Sunday Times newspaper that the influx of EU workers into Britain before Brexit had posed significant challenges.

“But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he said in a report released on Sunday.

“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, ‌since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things,” he said.

The issue of immigration was a key factor in the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign that ended with Britons narrowly voting to leave the EU.

A decade later, Burnham, who has even touted the possibility of Britain applying to rejoin the EU one day, said the country should have an “honest discussion” about how immigration to Britain has changed since Brexit.

Long-term net migration to the UK nearly halved ⁠in 2025 , according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), falling to 171,000 in 2025 from 331,000 a year earlier. This drop had not been seen since before the post-Brexit immigration system was introduced, as tougher government measures have restricted arrivals.

In his October 19 interview with The Sunday Times, Burnham said the issue of freedom of movement could be considered as part of a broader reset of the UK’s relationship with the EU, including on data sharing and migration.

“Consider what we’ve lost, which was the ability to be part of Eurodac and all the data collaboration around migration. You’ve got to see it in the round, rather than just looking at freedom of movement on its own,” he told The Sunday Times.

Nigel Farage, leader of the anti-immigration Reform UK party, called Burnham’s comments on free movement a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain”.

In his speech to the Labour Party conference last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” and called for Britain to consider its “long-term relationship” with the EU.

The prime minister, who is trying to find ways to ⁠speed up the UK economy, is due to meet top EU officials for ⁠a summit on November 20.

articles.title: Ralph Vaughan Williams' music royalties are funding a new generation of composers; four postgraduate students received £8,000 scholarships each in 2026
articles.summary: The music of British composer Ralph Vaughan Williams continues to support the next generation of musical talent through royalties that fund postgraduate
articles.body: The music of British composer Ralph Vaughan Williams continues to support the next generation of musical talent through royalties that fund postgraduate scholarships. In 2026, four students received £8,000 each from the Vaughan Williams Foundation to help finance their advanced studies in composition. The awards support aspiring composers who intend to build professional careers in music, continuing a tradition of backing emerging talent that has lasted for more than four decades. Through this initiative, the legacy of Vaughan Williams extends beyond his compositions.Vaughan Williams’ music royalties support postgraduate composersThe Vaughan Williams Foundation uses royalties earned from the composer’s music to support projects that benefit British musical life. According to the Foundation’s official website, the charity was established in 2022, 150 years after Vaughan Williams’ birth, by bringing together two trusts originally founded by the composer and his wife, Ursula Vaughan Williams.The Foundation’s work reflects Ralph Vaughan Williams’ interest in supporting fellow composers and making his own music accessible to the public. Its activities include funding performances, recordings and commissions, alongside educational and developmental opportunities for musicians.The Foundation’s postgraduate scholarship programme is an important part of this work. Rather than focusing only on preserving the achievements of an established composer, the funding also helps students develop the skills needed to contribute to contemporary music.Four students receive scholarships for the 2026-27 academic yearThe Foundation announced its 4 new Vaughan Williams Scholars in June 2026. According to its announcement, each recipient will receive £8,000 towards postgraduate composition studies during the 2026-27 academic year.The selected students are Patrick Gorry, who is studying at the Royal Northern College of Music, and Scarlett Henderson, who attends the Guildhall School of Music and Drama. The other recipients are Donnchadh Mac Aodha, a student at the Royal College of Music, and Dominic Wright, who is also studying at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama.The four awards represent a total commitment of £32,000 for the academic year. The funding is intended to contribute towards the costs of their studies as they develop their compositional abilities.In its announcement, the Foundation congratulated the recipients and expressed its hopes for a rewarding year ahead. It also encouraged audiences to look out for the emerging composers and their work.The awards form part of a longer-running initiative that has supported postgraduate composition students for more than 40 years. The Foundation’s website states that there have been 270 previous recipients, illustrating the programme’s reach across successive generations of musicians.Who can apply for the Vaughan Williams ScholarshipsThe scholarships are intended for applicants who demonstrate exceptional talent in composition and plan to make it their professional career.The funding is available towards the costs of a taught master’s degree or a PhD in composition at a university or conservatoire in the UK. Applicants must be British or Irish composers, or have lived continuously in the UK for at least 3 years. The Foundation also states that there is no age limit.These conditions allow the programme to support composers at different stages of their postgraduate education, provided they meet the eligibility requirements. However, the awards are designed for students pursuing composition as their main professional direction, rather than for musicians studying performance or other areas of music.The Foundation does not fund courses outside the UK, programmes focused on television, film or gaming composition, or courses devoted exclusively to electro-acoustic composition. Performance courses and research programmes centred on musicology or musical analysis are also excluded.According to the Foundation’s funding guidelines, each scholarship is awarded only once and cannot be renewed.The scholarship programme has developed to include doctoral studentsThe current scholarship scheme builds on an established tradition of postgraduate support. In its announcement about the programme’s development, the Foundation explained that the Vaughan Williams Scholarships were introduced in 2025 as a new funding opportunity for master’s and PhD students.The scholarships replaced the former Vaughan Williams bursaries for master’s students, expanding the opportunity to include doctoral study. This change created a funding route for eligible composers undertaking either a taught postgraduate degree or a research-based doctorate in composition.The Foundation’s 2025 scholarship announcement also highlighted the programme’s history of supporting composers who later developed significant careers. Previous recipients include Graham Fitkin, Julian Anderson, Christian Alexander, Anna Meredith, Larry Goves, Gavin Higgins, Hannah Kendall and Daniel Kidane.A musical legacy continues through new generationsThe Vaughan Williams Foundation supports more than postgraduate students. Its broader funding programme also helps finance performances, commissions and recordings by British and Irish composers, while supporting projects that increase public understanding of Ralph and Ursula Vaughan Williams.According to the Foundation’s main website, it has awarded more than £1.35 million to composer-related projects since 2023. The next round of Vaughan Williams Scholarships is scheduled to open in December 2026 for the 2027-28 academic year.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US midterms 2026: Meet Suhas Subramanyam, Indian-origin Democrat who served as advisor to Barack Obama

articles.body: Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia is among several Indian-origin candidates contesting the US midterm elections on November 3. The Democrat is seeking re-election from Virginia’s 10th Congressional District, where he faces Republican challenger Dave Beckwith, a 30-year veteran of the US Air Force.A lawyer by profession, Subramanyam served as a White House policy advisor during Barack Obama’s presidency.Family lifeBorn in Virginia in 1979, Subramanyam is the son of Indian immigrants. His mother, a Bengaluru native, moved to the US to join his father, who grew up in Chennai and Secunderabad, and to pursue higher education.Subramanyam is married to Miranda Pena Subramanyam, and the couple have two daughters. During his time in the state legislature, he passed legislation aimed at lowering tolls, utility bills and prescription drug costs. He also co-founded a caucus focused on bipartisanship and helped pass bipartisan bills on K-12 education, tax cuts and gun safety.Subramanyam was elected to represent Virginia’s 10th Congressional District in 2024, succeeding retiring Democratic incumbent Jennifer Wexton. articles.title: Trump's 250-foot Washington triumphal arch could begin construction Nov. 5; three veterans and an architectural historian have asked a federal judge to stop work without congressional approval
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington could see construction begin as early as November 5, according to news agency
articles.body: US President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington could see construction begin as early as November 5, according to news agency Associated Press. However, a group of military veterans and an architectural historian are trying to stop the project before work starts. The four have asked a federal judge to block construction, arguing that the administration must first obtain approval from Congress.November 5 is also the day when the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) is expected to consider the project's final plans. If the commission approves them and the remaining government requirements are completed, construction could begin that same day.The latest request was submitted on Thursday to US District Judge Tanya Chutkan. The plaintiffs include three veterans and a retired architectural historian. They are seeking a preliminary injunction, which is a temporary court order that can stop an activity while the legal dispute continues.The planned monument would stand in a traffic circle across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial, close to Arlington National Cemetery. Trump has proposed a structure measuring 250 feet, or about 76 metres, in height. Although the project has received some initial approvals, questions remain about whether those permissions are sufficient and whether the location is suitable for such a large monument.Opponents fear work may begin before rulingThe November 5 timeline became clear after the Justice Department submitted a notice to the court on October 21. The filing followed an earlier direction from Chutkan requiring the government to provide at least 14 days' notice before beginning construction.The government has outlined several conditions that must be met before work can start. Besides approval from the NCPC, the Interior Department must issue its final decision authorising construction. The National Park Service must also publish the required notification.Officials have indicated that these steps could be completed by November 5, making it the earliest possible date for construction.For those opposing the project, the concern is that construction could begin while the court is still considering the legality of the monument. Their filing argues that the administration has continued preparing for construction rather than waiting for the judicial process to conclude.The 1925 law at centre of the disagreementOne of the biggest questions in the case is whether a law passed more than a century ago gives the administration permission to build the arch today.The government has pointed to legislation signed by President Calvin Coolidge in 1925, which authorised the construction of Memorial Bridge. According to ABC News, the administration believes that the law also covers the proposed arch because the original plans for the bridge included columns at its end.The veterans and the architectural historian disagree. They argue that the 1925 legislation cannot be used as permission for the present monument and that Congress must specifically authorise its construction.They also say that officials have conducted site testing, prepared architectural designs and approached planning commissions while failing to seek approval from Congress.The US Commission of Fine Arts has already given the proposal preliminary approval. Its members were appointed by Trump, but the plaintiffs maintain that decisions by such commissions do not settle the question of congressional authorisation.Questions over the arch's design and locationApart from the legal dispute, the proposed monument has attracted attention because of its size and the additional purposes Trump has discussed for it.The president has previously suggested that the arch could accommodate security operations involving drones and snipers. However, the plans submitted by the Interior Department to the NCPC do not specifically describe the military complex he had mentioned. The department has said that the design could accommodate such a facility.There are also concerns about how the structure would affect its surroundings. In September, the administration acknowledged that the project would have adverse effects on the setting and views along the Potomac River. It nevertheless maintained that those effects could not be completely avoided because the chosen location was important to the proposal.Another legal challenge The lawsuit brought by the veterans and the historian is one of two cases challenging the arch. Earlier in October, the Arlington County Board in Virginia filed a separate case in the Eastern District of Virginia.The board questioned the pace at which the project was moving and argued that it had not undergone the full review process. The Trump administration has rejected that allegation.Meanwhile, Chutkan has directed the parties in the veterans' case to discuss and submit a schedule for further court filings by noon on Friday.The arch is among several Washington projects being pursued by Trump, including changes to a public golf course and proposals involving the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.You use AI every day. articles.title: British mum Leanne Gregory who died in Bahamas was celebrating wedding anniversary
articles.summary: Leanne Gregory, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, died trying to save her sons swept out to sea.
articles.body:
The husband of a woman who died as she tried to rescue her two sons when they were swept out to sea in the Bahamas said they had been celebrating their 10th wedding anniversary.

Leanne Gregory, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, had been on a family holiday with husband Nathan when he believes their boys were swept into the ocean by a riptide.

Although the children were rescued from the water on Tuesday, their mother was unable to be saved, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.

Speaking to the BBC on Sunday, Nathan, who is now back home with their sons, said the trip had been an early celebration for their anniversary in December.

He said both boys had been so excited and had been snorkelling in shallow water as they sorted out their towels and bags on the beach when the boys got into difficulties.

Both parents went into the sea and tried to save them as they were swept out by the current, he added, and the whole ordeal happened in less than 10 minutes.

Nathan said the loss of his 36-year-old "childhood sweetheart" was "unimaginable", but she was a "hero... in life and in death" as she helped to rescue the two boys.

"I've known her since infant school," he told the BBC. " We first got together when we were 14... so 22 years."

"There are no words I can use to describe Leanne, same as anyone she has ever known.

"She was the purest of people, the most generous kind and beautiful person who ever walked the earth.

"Our relationship was perfect. She was the perfect mother, the perfect wife the foundation of our entire family."

Nathan said: "Royal Caribbean and Virgin Airlines were absolutely incredible to us and made an impossible journey home so much easier.

Now, as he "keeps strong for his boys", a gofundme has generated nearly £9,000 in donations to support them.

More tributes have paid to the family since the tragedy.

Richard MacRae, who represents Stapleford north at Broxtowe Borough Council, said it was a "tight-knit community" that would rally around the family.

"It's sad, it's heartbreaking, when something tragic happens and people have got young kids involved, it is just a different level," he said.

"My thoughts and prayers are with the family and friends and the wider community."

On a BBC Facebook post, people passed on their condolences.

One post read: "Grateful to have known you and worked with you Leanne!

Stapleford Fire Station posted it was "deeply saddened" to hear of the mother of two's death.

They said: "Our thoughts are with her family and friends at this difficult time."

The two children were rescued off the coast of Bimini, police in the Bahamas said.

In a statement posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers received reports shortly after 10:00 local time on Tuesday that a woman had been found unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.

It added after she was swept away, she was brought to the ferry dock where CPR was given.

Leanne was then taken to a local medical clinic but was confirmed dead there, the police force said.

It said an autopsy would be conducted but "foul play is not suspected".

A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.

"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

articles.title: Mallikarjun Kharge’s 'baap' remark on PM Modi sparks row, BJP hits back
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge triggered a controversy on Sunday with his remark, “Modi ka baap bhi jayega” (Modi’s father will also be
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge triggered a controversy on Sunday with his remark, “Modi ka baap bhi jayega” (Modi’s father will also be defeated), at a programme in Patna.In a video shared by ANI, a person can be heard shouting, “Modi nahi jayega” (Modi will not be defeated), prompting a response from Kharge.“Modi ka baap bhi jayega … baap bhi jayega,” the Congress president retorted, as party workers escorted the person out of the hall.Targeting PM Modi further, Kharge called the prime minister a “habitual liar”.“PM Modi has a habit of telling lies. He had promised to bring back black money within his first 100 days. I want to ask, where is that money?” Kharge asked.BJP hits backThe BJP hit back, with Union home minister Amit Shah accusing Kharge of crossing all limits. Shah attributed the Congress’s “frustration” to its repeated electoral defeats since 2014."This is not the first time that the Congress party has used abusive language against Modi ji or his family. At times, they have used derogatory remarks about his revered mother; at other times, they have labelled him a 'maut ka saudagar' (merchant of death); and on other occasions, they have mocked his humble background by calling him a 'chaiwala' (tea seller). Under the leadership of Rahul Gandhi, the Congress party is crossing the boundaries of indecency with each passing day," Shah wrote in Hindi on X, referring to remarks by Congress leaders against the prime minister."Having faced consecutive electoral defeats over the past 12 years, the Congress party has become so mired in frustration and despair that it is now left with neither a coherent policy nor any substantive issues—only a politics of abuse. Having already lost public support, the Congress is now losing its footing even among its own party workers," he added.The home minister further stated that the public would give the Congress a “befitting reply”, as it had in the past whenever party leaders used alleged indecent language against PM Modi or his family.BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari attributed Kharge’s remarks to the Congress’s frustration over what he predicted would be a poor turnout at the party’s upcoming rally in Delhi.“Frustration of Congress is out in the open! Knowing its 1st November rally is about to be a flop show, knowing Rahul Gandhi's anarchy is being called out, knowing it is not getting support of People of India; Congress frustration is out in the open! Congress statement proves People of India are with PM Modi,” Bhandari posted on X.The Congress and its allies are scheduled to hold a rally at Delhi’s Ramlila Maidan on November 1 to protest alleged “vote chori” by the Election Commission in favour of the ruling BJP.Congress accuses BJP of 'disrespecting' Kharge againMeanwhile, the Congress alleged that the person who shouted "Modi nahi jayega" was a BJP worker and accused the party of "disrespecting" Kharge again after the alleged purification incident in Uttarakhand."Previously, they (BJP) engaged in a despicable act, so-called purification ritual in Uttarakhand, solely because he (Kharge) is a Dalit. Today, in Bihar, while Kharge ji was delivering a speech, a BJP worker rudely said that Modi will not go anywhere; even if your own father were to come," Congress MP Pawan Khera told ANI.Khera claimed that the Congress chief's "baap" reference was for the RSS, the BJP's ideological mentor, and RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat."In response, Kharge ji retorted that Modi will indeed go and so will his father referring to his ideological mentor: the Sangh, and Mohan Bhagwat. This repeated disrespect toward our national president is happening at the direct behest of Modi and Shah. The nation will not forgive this. The nation is watching," he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Cuba spent decades recruiting American spies. Now Washington is turning the tables on Havana
articles.summary: Marco Rubio's CIA invitation to Cuban insiders targets Havana's espionage apparatus, pressuring a dictatorship that recruited spies like Ana Belén Montes.
articles.body: Cuba’s government has spent decades recruiting Americans to betray their country. It objects to Secretary of State Marco Rubio inviting Cubans to cooperate with the CIA. Havana apparently believes espionage should remain a privilege of the dictatorship. The Trump administration is right to disagree. Rubio is challenging a comfortable assumption in Washington: that Cuba is too broke to matter. A regime unable to keep the lights on can still penetrate a government, compromise an intelligence officer, and help America’s adversaries. Poverty has never disqualified a country from espionage. It can make espionage one of its more valuable exports. I am an American of Cuban descent who spent more than two decades as a CIA operations officer, including service as chief of station in Latin America. That background leaves me with little patience for the assumption that a failing economy must produce an incompetent security apparatus. Dictatorships allocate resources according to what keeps them in power. Feeding the population and protecting the regime are different priorities. Havana has made its choice repeatedly. CUBA’S ECONOMIC FREEFALL IS HIDING A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT JUST MILES FROM FLORIDA: REPORT The record requires little elaboration. Ana Belén Montes became the Pentagon’s leading Cuba analyst while working for Cuban intelligence. She exposed American intelligence officers and distorted Washington’s understanding of the country she was supposed to assess. Victor Manuel Rocha served as a U.S. ambassador and on the National Security Council while secretly serving Havana. Kendall and Gwendolyn Myers sustained an espionage conspiracy for 30 years. These were patient investments in access. Cuban intelligence cultivated ideological commitment, steered recruits toward useful positions, and allowed American institutions to supply salaries, credentials, and trust. Montes needed no fortune deposited offshore. Conviction was enough. The most damaging agent may be the respected expert whose colleagues cannot imagine that his judgment belongs to someone else. ALLEGED CUBAN INFLUENCE OPERATIVE, FAMILY IN FEDERAL CUSTODY AFTER RUBIO REVOKES LEGAL STATUS The consequences extended beyond stolen documents. Cuba’s Wasp Network penetrated exile organizations and targeted American military facilities. One of its officers was convicted of conspiracy to commit murder in connection with the 1996 destruction of two Brothers to the Rescue aircraft. Four men died, three of them American citizens. Havana’s intelligence operations have carried a human cost that diplomatic euphemisms cannot erase. Rubio’s invitation puts pressure where it belongs: on the people who keep the regime functioning. An intelligence officer, military official, or party insider may know which Americans Havana has recruited, which foreign services it assists, or who signed an order to arrest a dissident. That knowledge gives him something to offer. Washington should make clear that it is prepared to listen. FLORIDA ATTORNEY GENERAL JAMES UTHMEIER SECURES STATE ARREST WARRANT FOR RAÚL CASTRO The invitation also puts a question inside Cuban headquarters that no security chief can comfortably dismiss: Who among us has already answered? Even suspicion can consume time and manpower. Every officer assigned to investigate a colleague is an officer unavailable for another mission. A service accustomed to exploiting American trust should have to spend more effort defending its own. The work behind that invitation must be exacting. Havana will send fabricators and sources it controls. A volunteer’s hatred of the regime does not establish that his information is true. Verify what he knows, test what he claims, and protect him if he proves reliable. The measure of success is a Cuban agent inside an American institution identified, a threatened source protected, or a Cuban operation stopped. US SANCTIONS FIVE CUBAN ENTITIES, CASTRO FAMILY MEMBER IN LATEST PRESSURE CAMPAIGN, RUBIO SAYS The president needs to know who works for Havana inside our institutions, what its partners receive, and where its chain of command is vulnerable. A negotiator who knows what the other side is concealing is harder to deceive. A counterintelligence service that can identify the next Montes before she spends years in place can prevent damage that no prosecution will undo. That is the return on patient intelligence work. Havana will call cooperation with Washington treason. A dictatorship always finds it convenient to confuse its own survival with the life of the nation. Cubans who expose the officials imprisoning their neighbors or the intelligence networks threatening other countries need no lecture on patriotism from the people responsible. The regime does not own their allegiance merely because it controls their passports. CUBA'S FOREIGN MINISTER ACCUSES MARCO RUBIO OF LYING TO AMERICANS TO JUSTIFY ACTION AGAINST CUBA President Donald Trump and Rubio are right to force this choice. Pressure should make service to the regime more costly, while a credible opening gives insiders a reason to leave it. Washington must sustain both long enough to produce results. articles.title: In 1834, a historic Métis family home was built beside Georgian Bay in Canada; 192 years later, its owner transferred it for just $2 and the 75,000-pound house was moved across the water for a planned museum
articles.summary: An 1834 Métis home built near the Canadian shoreline is beginning a new chapter after being moved across Georgian Bay.
articles.body: An 1834 Métis home built near the Canadian shoreline is beginning a new chapter after being moved across Georgian Bay. Its private owner sold the historic building for just $2 to help create a heritage museum. Known as the Labatte House, the building weighs about 75,000 pounds. It was placed on a special barge at Thunder Beach, Ontario, and carried across the water to Balm Beach. The move aims to protect what is believed to be Ontario’s oldest surviving historic Métis home. Louis-George Labatte and his family built the timber and stone house in 1834. It offers a direct link to the early history of settlement around the Great Lakes. The Métis Nation of Ontario organised the move to protect the building from damage caused by age or possible redevelopment of the original site.Navigating the shoreline journeyMoving a historic building weighing 75,000 pounds across open water required careful planning and special equipment. Moving crews used hydraulic jacks and steel beams to lift the single-storey house from its original foundations. Once the house was raised, the crew moved it onto a heavy-duty transport trailer. They then drove it onto a large barge waiting near the shore at Thunder Beach. The barge carried the building across Georgian Bay towards Balm Beach. Weather conditions along the bay needed close attention throughout the journey. Strong winds and rough waves could have affected the balance of the barge and put the building at risk. The vessel reached Balm Beach safely, where workers unloaded the house for transport over land.Securing a cultural havenThe decision to move the house was driven by limits at its original location. Thunder Beach had offered a suitable home for the Labatte family in 1834, but the privately owned site lacked enough space and facilities for public visits, parking and long-term preservation work. Recognising the building's historical importance, the private owner agreed to sell it to the Métis Nation of Ontario for the symbolic price of $2. The house was moved to a 39-acre property at 159 Balm Beach Road East. The larger site offers space for restoring the land, creating walking trails and building modern educational facilities around the historic home. Saving the house is about more than protecting an old building. Organisers say physical reminders of early Métis settlement are rare across the Great Lakes region. "We cannot replace this. This is a living testimony to the fact that the Métis here in Ontario existed, and that we still exist," said Mitch Anderson, a representative speaking on behalf of the preservation project, in comments reported by news outlet Collingwood Today.Establishing the museum siteWorkers have placed the house on a temporary support frame at the Balm Beach property. Plans call for a permanent concrete foundation to be poured in spring 2027. After that, restoration work will focus on the timber frame, roof and stonework inside the building. Once the work is complete, the house will become the main feature of a planned museum and cultural centre dedicated to Indigenous and Métis history in the region. Exhibits are expected to include 19th-century trade tools, household objects and historical documents that tell the story of the Métis community around Georgian Bay. The Métis Nation of Ontario has confirmed plans to apply for official municipal heritage designation through the Township of Tiny once the house is placed on its permanent foundation. This status would offer legal protection against future demolition or changes to the building's structure. Community members and descendants of the Labatte family gathered at the new site in Balm Beach to mark the house's safe arrival. articles.title: America's little-known castles, displaying 'raw power,' are hiding in plain sight
articles.summary: Author and historian Dan Jones traces 3,000 years of fortifications in "Castles," from Fort Sumter and Fort Pulaski to the Tower of London's gruesome dark history.
articles.body: When most Americans think of castles, they likely picture medieval fortresses towering over European hills. Yet the history of these imposing structures is much closer to home than many might realize. Speaking to Fox News Digital from England, historian Dan Jones described his latest book as a 3,000-year journey through human history, from the Sack of Troy to the Nuclear Age, as it explores the broader history of castles and fortifications. DIVERS UNCOVER ANCIENT TREASURES LINKED TO ROMAN GIANT WHO HELPED SHAPE AMERICAN HISTORY From Iron Age hillforts to classic medieval castles and beyond, "Castles: A Fortified History of the World," explores fortifications across different eras and regions of the world, including Japan's Himeji Castle and nuclear bunkers built during the Cold War. Jones examines the role America has played in the broader history of castles, from early fortifications to Civil War-era forts. "I don't think we can truly understand it without having the American side to the story," said Jones. One notable example is Fort Sumter in South Carolina, where Confederate forces opened fire on Union troops in April 1861, marking the beginning of the Civil War. 'HIGHLY UNUSUAL' CANNONBALL CACHE FOUND AT CONSTRUCTION SITE IN COASTAL CITY MAY BE WORLD'S FIRST Jones described Fort Sumter, a coastal fortress built with thick brick walls and artillery defenses, as one of the "descendants of castles" that emerged in America. Another important moment in the history of castle building, Jones said, came when Union forces attacked Fort Pulaski in Georgia with rifled cannons in 1862. The fort had been considered nearly impenetrable, but was "blown to bits" within 48 hours, Jones told Fox News Digital. "Fort Pulaski was just thought to be so strong, you may as well bombard the Rocky Mountains," Jones said. RARE CANNONBALL EMERGES FROM GROUND AT THE ALAMO, LIKELY UNTOUCHED FOR NEARLY 190 YEARS "Well, Fort Pulaski was blown to bits in 48 hours, and that was a transformative moment in the whole history of castle building." Beyond military forts, America is also home to grand, castle-like estates built as displays of wealth and status, including Hearst Castle in California and Gilded Age mansions such as the Biltmore Estate in North Carolina and Belcourt in Newport, Rhode Island. Asked about the historical significance of America's grand, castle-like estates, Jones said that castles have long served two purposes: providing defense and displaying wealth and power. "There's this moment in the Middle Ages where they're combined, but you can see this in America today." In that respect, many of the grand estates built during America's Gilded Age followed the same tradition as the magnificent residences of medieval kings and nobles. "There's this moment in the Middle Ages where they're combined, but you can see this in America today," Jones said. "There are colossal fortifications and there are these colossal palatial houses that have always been built by the super wealthy." He pointed to Disneyland's Sleeping Beauty Castle, built in 1955, as another example of the enduring appeal of castles in the popular imagination. "These are as much a part of the story of castles as the sort of classic medieval ... stronghold," he said. "The castle can sit on the landscape to intimidate, to terrify, to be a display of raw power," he said. The history of castles is, of course, also filled with gruesome details, and some of the most famous fortresses served as prisons and sites of torture and execution. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Jones pointed to the Tower of London, where Anne Boleyn was beheaded and Guy Fawkes was tortured following the Gunpowder Plot of 1605. "I've had dinner in the room in which Guy Fawkes was stretched out on the rack after the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, which is a slightly grisly place to be," Jones told Fox News Digital. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ But castles have also served as zoos, mints and royal residences, Jones noted. Despite their sometimes dark history, Jones believes the enduring fascination with castles goes beyond what meets the eye. "Somewhere deep down the story of the castle is the story of building places to protect the things we love," he said. articles.title: In 2019, New York changed the law to let survivors pursue decades-old abuse claims; seven years later, about 1,300 people have agreed to an $800 million settlement with the Catholic archdiocese, pending signatures
articles.summary: The Catholic Archdiocese of New York has agreed to pay $800 million (£615 million) to around 1,300 survivors who reported sexual abuse by clergy and other
articles.body: The Catholic Archdiocese of New York has agreed to pay $800 million (£615 million) to around 1,300 survivors who reported sexual abuse by clergy and other church staff. The settlement brings years of legal disputes and negotiations closer to an end. Lawyers representing the survivors announced the agreement. It covers a large number of civil lawsuits filed under a New York state law that temporarily allowed people to bring claims over historical sexual abuse, even when the usual time limit for legal action had passed. Both sides have agreed to the main terms of the financial settlement. However, lawyers said the final documents still need to be processed and formally signed before payments can be made to individual survivors.Legal changes opened path to justiceThe legal action began to grow in 2019, when New York lawmakers passed the Child Victims Act. The law created a temporary period during which adults who had experienced sexual abuse as children could file civil lawsuits, even if the alleged abuse had happened decades earlier. Before the law changed, strict time limits had stopped many people from taking legal action against religious institutions, schools and youth organisations. The temporary window led to thousands of lawsuits across New York State against Catholic dioceses, including the Archdiocese of New York. The archdiocese covers Manhattan, the Bronx, Staten Island and seven nearby counties. The large number of claims created financial and legal pressure for several dioceses. Some other Catholic dioceses in New York sought protection from creditors through federal bankruptcy proceedings. The Archdiocese of New York, based in Manhattan, instead tried to settle the claims without entering formal Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings.Distribution and oversight mechanismsThe $800 million settlement was put together using money from archdiocesan assets, contributions from affiliated religious orders and insurance payments. Under the agreement reached by the lawyers, each survivor's payment will be decided through an independent review process. Administrators will consider the seriousness of the reported abuse, its long-term emotional and physical effects, and the historical records available to support each claim. Lawyers representing the survivors said the amounts would differ among the 1,300 claimants. The money is intended to help cover medical costs, psychological counselling and damages linked to the abuse. The agreement also includes steps aimed at improving transparency. The archdiocese agreed to release more internal records about clergy members who have been credibly accused of abuse. It also agreed to keep public records updated, with the aim of helping prevent similar cases from being hidden in the future.Impact on local church operationsThe settlement will be funded through church reserves, property transactions and insurance payments. The $800 million payout is among the largest single financial settlements agreed by a Catholic jurisdiction in United States history. Cardinal Timothy Dolan, the Archbishop of New York, has previously recognised the serious harm caused by historical abuse within the Church. He described the offences as a dark period in the institution's history and pledged to co-operate with oversight measures. The agreement is expected to help the archdiocese resolve hundreds of pending cases in New York state courts. Many of these lawsuits had remained open since the Child Victims Act took effect in 2019. Representatives for the survivors said that no amount of money could erase the trauma they had experienced. However, they said the settlement offered financial support and a measure of accountability for people who had waited years for their cases to be addressed, including those now reaching older age. The agreement still requires final signatures and the completion of court approval procedures. These steps are expected to be completed over the coming months, after which payments can be arranged for individual claimants.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: "Nobody Wants This" creator Erin Foster responded to the show's star Adam Brody accusing Israel of "genocide," saying she disagrees with him and defended the show.
articles.body: The creator of Netflix's "Nobody Wants This," Erin Foster, disagrees with the show's star, Adam Brody, over his support for a "free Palestine" and accusing Israel of "genocide," while emphasizing that it was "OK" for them to have different opinions. "You know, it’s complicated," Foster said when asked about Brody's comments on the "Not Skinny But Not Fat" podcast. "I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing." "While I love Adam, I also disagree with him and that's OK. I think that as the creator of the show, all I can say is that I want our Jewish fans to know that I see you and I hear you and I understand how you feel," Foster said. The full episode of the podcast interview with Foster is set to air on Oct. 27. Brody accused Israel of "genocide" during a September interview with GQ and said he supported a "free Palestine." WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM Foster said the show has always been a love letter to Judaism. "That is why I made this show. It's because of how beautiful of an experience I've had becoming Jewish and being a Jewish person and sitting here right now at this time in the world where there is almost zero positive representation of Jewish people. I think it's so important to have that and that is what this show is intended to be," she said. The "Nobody Wants This" creator also said that people can have their own opinions. "And that being said, everyone is entitled to a different opinion than me. I can just tell you what I created this show for and what the intention of the show is," Foster added. DEBRA MESSING OPENS UP ON ANTISEMITISM, OCTOBER 7 AND BACKLASH OVER PRO-ISRAEL STANCE Fox News Digital has reached out to Brody's team for comment. Mor Greenberg, founder of MorMedia Group, a public relations and strategic communications firm that works with numerous Jewish nonprofits, pro-Israel organizations and advocacy groups, told Fox News Digital in a statement, "It's disappointing to finally see a mainstream television show celebrating Jewish identity, only to have its leading actor make headlines for comments that are deeply upsetting to many in the Jewish community." Greenberg said there was enormous pressure in Hollywood to take a "fashionable position" on Israel, but "very little room for anyone who dares to defend it." She said while Brody is entitled to his political views, "playing a rabbi on television doesn't make him a spokesperson for the Jewish community." "That's why I appreciate Erin Foster's response. She understands that Jewish identity is bigger than Hollywood politics, and she isn't afraid to stand behind the Jewish story she created. At a time when positive Jewish representation is so desperately needed, that matters," Greenberg continued. I'm hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is." articles.title: How is the US-Israeli war on Iran causing havoc in Europe?
articles.summary: Rising energy costs and protests are sharpening European opposition to renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
articles.body:
Several Western European nations have expressed their opposition to the potential resumption of the Iran war, as spiralling global oil prices have worsened the cost of living crisis across Europe.

Countries such as Germany and the UK, among other major powers, which initially remained silent on the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran, have aired their views, calling for diplomacy to end the war which has disrupted global oil supplies.

Continued disruption to energy supplies is pushing up household costs as winter in Europe approaches, adding fuel to protests over living standards that have engulfed European capitals in recent weeks.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Sunday drew attention to what he described as a shift in Germany’s position on attacks against Iran.

In a post on X, Baghaei recalled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s remarks during Israel’s June 2025 military campaign: “This is the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.”

He contrasted those words with German officials’ recent warnings against renewed attacks and calls to prevent further escalation, before citing Friedrich Schiller’s The Maid of Orleans, quoting a passage that portrays reason being helplessly dragged towards an abyss by the forces of madness.

Experts say Baghaei’s remarks reflect a broader shift across Europe, where leaders are increasingly questioning their support for the US-Israeli war on Iran.

With Washington reportedly preparing options for renewed attacks, what would further escalation mean for Europe and could the war further strain already frayed relations with the United States?

When the US and Israel launched their attacks on February 28 , the leaders of Britain, France and Germany issued a joint statement condemning Iran’s retaliatory strikes on countries across the region. “We condemn Iranian attacks on countries in the region in the strongest terms,” British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, French President Emmanuel Macron and Merz said.

Their statement did not condemn the opening US-Israeli attacks. However, it called for negotiations to follow. Nearly eight months into the war, European governments are now explicitly warning against another military campaign.

On Friday, the foreign ministers of Britain, France, Germany and Italy met their counterparts from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt in Istanbul to discuss the conflict and the Strait of Hormuz. Further escalation between Iran and the US “would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.

“And so the first thing this group of eight countries … will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region,” he added.

The warnings against new attacks do not necessarily mean European governments have abandoned their positions on Iran’s nuclear programme or regional activities, but they do show a change of position and have revealed that European governments are not united in their approach to the Iran war.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has consistently opposed the US-Israeli campaign. At this month’s European summit, he again described the war as “illegal, unjust and unjustified”, linking it to Europe’s mounting economic costs.

Western countries have opposed Iran’s nuclear programme, which Tehran says is for civilian purposes only. European countries were part of the landmark 2015 nuclear deal with Iran that limited Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief. But during his first term in 2018, United States President Donald Trump withdrew from the deal. Both the US and Israel invoked Iran’s nuclear programme to launch their attack in February.

Europe’s divisions have been particularly visible over access to military bases and airspace. “We did not participate in these strikes, but are in close contact with our international partners, including the United States, Israel and partners in the region,” said the February 28 statement from Britain, France and Germany.

But non-participation in the opening attacks did not mean European countries would uniformly refuse support for subsequent operations. Germany said early in the war that it would not restrict US use of its bases, including Ramstein, a major American military hub.

Britain initially withheld permission for the opening attacks. However, it authorised US use of British bases for what London described as specific, limited defensive strikes against Iranian facilities involved in attacks on regional allies. Then, after initial reluctance, Britain expanded that permission to include operations against missile sites and capabilities being used to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

France allowed US support aircraft at Istres, while saying they would support the defence of regional partners rather than participate in attacks on Iran. It later blocked a weapons flight to Israel connected to the campaign. Spain went further. After refusing permission for attacks from the jointly operated Rota and Moron bases, Madrid closed its airspace to US aircraft involved in the war.

Those were different restrictions with different purposes, rather than a single European refusal to cooperate, but they provoked Trump. Calling Spain “terrible”, he threatened to cut off trade and said Washington wanted “nothing to do with Spain”.

The dispute has therefore exposed a widening argument over whether alliance commitments require European governments to facilitate a war they did not choose.

Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera: “As to whether the war might push European leaders to openly challenge Trump, and limit support, it is certainly possible. What was initially a diplomatic disagreement is turning into something that has much more direct … and we could see increased resistance to any support from European countries.”

After Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening strikes, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said there was “renewed hope for the people of Iran”. She also warned then that instability could push the region into a spiral of violence. But by October 16, the costs to Europe had become central to her message. “Households and industry are paying the price for a war far beyond our borders,” she said after an EU summit.

According to von der Leyen, Europe’s bill for imported fossil fuels had increased by 106 billion euros, while gas prices had risen about 140 percent since late February and diesel prices had doubled.

Disruption to Gulf supplies and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have also caused energy prices to spike. Brent crude settled at $72.48 a barrel on February 27, before the war began. It reached $126.41 at the end of April and remains well above $100 a barrel, with no sign of falling any time soon.

“For Europe, there is the economic interest as well, knowing it would further take a toll on energy markets, pushing up prices at a time when European countries are going into winter and the pushback to that,” Julie Norman, an associate fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.

Hilborne added that “there is an impact as well on food and fertiliser … The Persian Gulf is a hub for nitrogen-based fertilisers and disruptions have sent prices of urea up by something like 70 percent. Also, supply chains are feeling the impact as well, as shipping companies are facing large increases in their insurance premiums and/or need to reroute to longer journeys”.

“I would say that the Iranian war has had a direct, measurable and quite a rapid impact on European prices,” he added.

The search for relief from the energy crisis has created further friction, with Washington pressing European governments to release emergency diesel stocks, while Trump eased restrictions on Russian diesel in an effort to lower prices. That move provoked criticism from Ukraine and its supporters, who warned that renewed energy revenues would strengthen Moscow’s war effort.

But some of the sharpest political consequences are unfolding closer to home. Protests over living costs, housing, wages and public services have been seen across France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece and Albania. Their causes vary, and they do not constitute a single coordinated movement, but experts say the cost of living crisis, compounded by price rises caused by the Iran war, is a common thread that unites the protesters across the continent.

Donatella della Porta, a sociologist and political scientist, told Al Jazeera that opposition to war was central to recent protests by young people across Europe, alongside anger over military spending at the expense of welfare.

She pointed to opposition to military recruitment in schools, weapons-related university research and the use of ports to transport arms, linking those concerns to wider fears about the future.

“Especially the young protesters are afraid that their future will be stolen not only by global warming but also by wars in which they will be sent to die on the battlefield,” she said.

“Young people also connect wars with genocide, having often been socialised into politics during the large protests against the Israeli genocide of the Palestinians.”

articles.title: Six Flags to add seat belts to roller coasters after Georgia rider’s death
articles.summary: Six Flags is overhauling lap restraints on coasters across the U.S. and Canada, but key details about reopening timelines remain unanswered.
articles.body: Six Flags is adding seat belts to several of its roller coasters after a Georgia man’s fatal fall on a ride that relied on lap restraints to keep passengers in their seats. The safety overhaul comes less than two weeks after 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was ejected from the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. Eight other Six Flags coasters with similar restraint systems remain closed across the U.S. and Canada as investigators work to determine what went wrong. Witnesses said they saw Kariem rise out of his seat and fall headfirst back into the cart before being ejected from the ride on Oct. 12. Some passengers who rode Goliath earlier that day also reported concerns about its restraints. ATTORNEY SAYS FATAL SIX FLAGS ROLLER COASTER ACCIDENT COULD RAISE BROADER SAFETY QUESTIONS AS 9 RIDES CLOSE The restraint system, manufactured by Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard, was designed to give riders the sensation of sitting on a "flying carpet" while still "guaranteeing optimum security," according to a U.S. patent granted to the company in 2001. Now, Six Flags says it is taking additional precautions. "We are reinforcing safety precautions at our parks and taking additional measures, including adding seat belts on Goliath and other coasters with a similar restraint," Six Flags Entertainment President and CEO John Reilly said in a statement Friday. Six Flags has not said which other coasters will get seat belts or when the closed rides might reopen. COLLEGE GRAD REPORTEDLY DIES IN SIX FLAGS ROLLER COASTER INCIDENT AS FAMILY SUES THEME PARK All nine coasters taken out of service were made by Bolliger & Mabillard. Each uses a padded restraint that locks over a rider's lap and upper legs, held in place by a bar between the knees. Six Flags said it has enlisted independent engineers and inspectors to review safety procedures across its theme parks. The eight additional roller coasters remain closed at Six Flags parks in Illinois, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio and Ontario, Canada. Goliath also remains shut down as state and local officials investigate Kariem's death. The fatal incident prompted precautionary closures beyond Six Flags properties. articles.title: Aneurin Bevan and how the Query Club set him on path to power
articles.summary: How a group of young radicals helped set Aneurin Bevan on the path to founding the NHS.
articles.body:
In the winter of 1921, a group of men gathered in a café in a small working class town.

Almost all were colliers used to the hard life hacking coal from the rich seams of the south Wales valleys - the region that had powered the industrial revolution and underpinned the growth and wealth of the global British Empire.

But few of the benefits of that wealth had trickled down to the people who produced it.

These men met in Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, to debate how could they change that.

This was the launch of the Query Club, a semi-secret society that began examining socialist ideas and ended as a force which changed their town – and later, through their ideas, the whole country.

One of those young debaters was Aneurin Bevan, the man who would go on to found the NHS and revolutionise housing for ordinary people when he became minister for health and housing two decades later.

It was revealed recently that MI5 followed him from around this time for 20 years, considering Bevan a firebrand left-winger linked to prominent communists .

In the 1920s, Tredegar was a town like many in south Wales.

Private collieries and iron works held a grip over the working people, with owners and managers powerful in local institutions such as the town council and hospital board.

Bevan, the son of a miner, had spent time underground and was all too familiar with the lack of control ordinary people had over their working lives and living conditions.

The Query Club gradually came to realise that if they wanted to change things, they had to be where the power was.

"The Query Club was this organisation which was Bevan and his comrades asking 'how do we actually achieve change here in Tredegar? How do we try to influence things?'," said Dr Nye Davies.

"I think they decided what we need to do is be on every single committee, every single board, every single institution that has some level of influence in the community and we need to get like-minded socialists on to those boards."

Davies, a senior lecturer at Cardiff University who was written books on Bevan, believes the search for power was central to everything the Query Club wanted to achieve.

One of its leading figures was Walter Conway, the only member over 30, and an orphan raised in the local workhouse.

Rather against the popular perception of neglect and brutality the name often evokes, the master of the house had taught Conway to read and write and given him a lifelong love of learning.

This was something he shared in common with Bevan.

In 1915, Conway beat 50 other applicants to become secretary of t he Tredegar Medical Aid Society .

As in other towns, workers formed the society by contributing a small payment from their wages, to cover costs when medical needs arose.

During Conway's time in charge, the society expanded from a membership of 5,000 at its start to 20,000 by the time of his death in 1933, representing 95% of the town.

They had access to doctors, nurses, dentists, and hospitals.

Wives, children and non-miners were all admitted, changing this health service for workers into a universal one – for Tredegar, at least.

The other change was led by the Query Club.

They knew all the important institutions of the town – the council, the hospital board, the workingmen's club, even the medical aid society itself – were dominated by board members who belonged to the major power in the town, the Tredegar Iron and Coal Company, with an interest in keeping power in the hands of the well-to-do.

As members of the emerging Labour party and committed socialists, they set their sights on changing that.

John Morgan, a local councillor and the great-nephew of one of the 20 members of the Query Club, still lives in Tredegar and has researched its history.

The Workman's Institute, where the club would eventually meet following its early days in cafes, is long gone.

But the Medical Aid Society building now houses the Tredegar Medical Aid Society Heritage Centre.

A small meeting room at the back is dedicated to the Query Club, with photographs and information preserving its memory.

"I used to go out walking with my uncle when he was in his 80s and 90s," he explained.

"He died when I was about 12 but if I knew then what I know now I'd have spent hours talking to him about the Query Club because some of the things they got up to - they were radicals."

In 1922, they put Bevan up for the town council, and by 1929, the 16 members comprised of 10 from Labour, with five of these members of the Query Club.

Through the 1920s, Query Club members and others sympathetic to their thinking gained key seats in the town's institutions.

They were, however, "very selective" on who could join the club, and be permitted to wear the club's badge with its signature question mark.

"People knew that the Query Club existed but when they would ask them 'what does the badge mean?' they would say 'oh, that's the question'," Morgan said.

"You weren't allowed to tell people what happened in the club.

"They infiltrated a lot of organisations but they would go through a series of tests and interviews before they allowed anybody to become a member."

It was all aimed at reducing the influence of the established authorities.

Bevan moved on to the next level of power by being elected to the county council, in Newport.

But as Davies explains, he realised this still wasn't enough, adding: "Bevan said 'power is still eluding us, it's still elsewhere'.

"And that's what led him to go to Parliament as the ultimate place where power lay.

"That quest for power was really what drove the Query Club, what really drove Bevan and inspired him for the rest of his career."

In 1929, he was elected as MP for Ebbw Vale, and went to Westminster, where he quickly gained a reputation as a powerful speaker.

Davies partly credits the Query Club with helping create Bevan the orator.

"These debates and arguments over ideas were really important in shaping Bevan's outlook as well," he added.

"One of Bevan's strengths was his debating skills and his ability to deconstruct arguments."

Images of Bevan, Tredegar's most famous son, adorn the shelves and wall of the heritage centre.

But Morgan says many members of the Query Club went on hold positions of influence for decades.

"There was Archie Lush, who became Sir Archie, who was his [Bevan's] agent, and there were other locals who became local councillors, mayors," he said.

Written on the walls of the heritage centre is the quote attributed to Bevan about creating the NHS in 1948: "We will Tredegarise you."

Davies believes this is probably apocryphal and never actually said by Bevan, but adds: "It does explain the legacy of the Tredegar Medical Aid society, that this was the foundation for the NHS."

articles.title: From arrests to crackdowns, how Europe’s leaders are responding as protests rock the continent
articles.summary: Emmanuel Macron vows rioters will pay as 70,000 police deploy across France, while Italy, Belgium and Albania face escalating protest violence.
articles.body: From mass arrests in France to troop deployments in Italy, European leaders are taking varied approaches to protests and clashes across the continent. The unrest began in France in mid-September with student demonstrations over school conditions, then spread to other countries, where protests have centered on local grievances. President Donald Trump has used the unrest to press his hard-line immigration message, blaming France’s protests on immigration and urging the country to close its borders. PHOTOS SHOW AFTERMATH OF RIOTS AS MASKED GROUPS CLASH WITH POLICE ACROSS FRANCE French President Emmanuel Macron pushed back, calling foreign leaders' comments "unacceptable and even stupid" and accusing them of exploiting France’s crisis for political gain. Here’s how leaders across Europe are responding. France vows to make rioters pay as cities assess damage Macron has vowed that those who loot or destroy property will be held accountable and made to pay for the damage. French authorities deployed 70,000 police officers nationwide Saturday as demonstrations took place in Paris and other cities. Some clashes broke out in several cities, including Paris, Lyon, Lille, Toulouse and Nantes. Police used tear gas, sound grenades and water cannons, and the Interior Ministry reported more than 1,300 arrests. VIOLENCE ERUPTS AT FRANCE PROTESTS AS MACRON WARNS UNREST IS BEING EXPLOITED Most union-organized marches were peaceful, though clashes broke out later in Paris and several other cities. Separately, a French intelligence assessment reportedly identified Antifa and other far-left groups as instigators of some of the violence, according to a French outlet. Italy takes one of Europe's toughest lines Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned what she called "gangs of thugs" who used demonstrations to "sow chaos," and voiced support for police facing violence in several Italian cities. Meloni moved quickly after the previous weekend’s looting and clashes, sending 500 additional soldiers to Milan and approving tougher penalties for minors involved in vandalism. She said destroying and stealing was a crime and that the state's response would be firm. The measures put Meloni among the European leaders taking the most visible steps to deter further violence. Greek police maintain a visible presence While Greece has seen less unrest than France and other European countries, officials have been monitoring the risk of clashes as student and teacher demonstrations spread. Government spokesperson Pavlos Marinakis said the right to protest must be respected as long as demonstrations remain lawful, while condemning violence, looting and occupations. Police still kept a visible presence at demonstrations earlier in the week, which largely passed without major violence. Belgium accuses Antifa-linked activists of stoking clashes Belgium's demonstrations began over education reforms and budget cuts, with young protesters taking to the streets in Brussels and Liège. Earlier clashes injured police, damaged public areas and blocked roads. Nearly 200 people were arrested, according to Belgian officials. Interior Minister Bernard Quintin accused far-left activists, including people linked to Antifa, of infiltrating demonstrations and encouraging young people to commit violence. Albania clashes escalate as protesters demand prime minister's ouster In Albania’s capital, Tirana, student-led protests have grown into a broader challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama, with demonstrators demanding his resignation and accusing his government of corruption and neglecting schools and public services. US LAWMAKERS SOUND ALARM AS VIOLENCE GRIPS NATO ALLY ALBANIA AMID ANTI-GOVERNMENT PROTESTS Police used tear gas and water cannons as more than 2,500 officers were deployed. Rama placed chairs outside his government headquarters and invited protesters to talk, but they rejected the gesture. He said his government would address their concerns and warned that people responsible for violence could face criminal and financial consequences. Spanish regional leaders vow consequences after Barcelona riots In Spain, the unrest was largely concentrated in Barcelona, unlike France, where protests and clashes spread across multiple cities. Police arrested 128 people in Barcelona after fires, vandalism and looting. Catalonia, the northeastern Spanish region that includes Barcelona, saw its regional president, Salvador Illa, condemn the violence and back the police response. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP Meanwhile, Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni said the city would take legal action against those responsible and warned that parents or guardians could face consequences for damage caused by their children.
